outcome.shown: A bicycle stays upright primarily through a combination of its steering geometry and the active steering inputs of the rider. When a bicycle begins to lean to one side, its steering geometry—specifically the "trail," which causes the front wheel to act like a self-aligning caster—naturally turns the front wheel in the direction of the lean. This steering action, whether initiated automatically by the bike's design or actively by the rider, steers the wheels back under the bicycle's center of mass, generating a corrective centrifugal force that pushes the bike upright. While the gyroscopic effect of the spinning wheels provides a minor amount of stability at higher speeds, it is this continuous process of steering into the direction of the fall that is the fundamental mechanism keeping the bicycle balanced.
